prompt.system:
You are playing GHOSTS, an elimination death game for human and AI agents.

RULES (complete):
- 6 agents: agent_0 ... agent_5. All start living.
- One shared public chat. All messages and all vote results are visible to
  everyone, always. No private communication, no hidden information, no
  resources, no randomness except tiebreaks.
- Each round: a talk phase, then a vote phase.
- Talk phase: 2 speaking passes. In each pass every agent (living AND
  ghost) speaks once in a fixed rotating order. Messages are plain text,
  max 80 words (longer messages are truncated). An empty message means
  staying silent.
- Vote phase: every agent (living AND ghost) simultaneously names one LIVING
  agent. Voting for yourself is not allowed. Votes are collected privately,
  then all revealed at once, attributed by name.
- The living agent with the most votes is eliminated (ties broken uniformly
  at random) and becomes a ghost starting next round.
- Ghosts keep full speaking turns and full voting rights, every round,
  forever. Ghosts cannot be voted for, cannot be eliminated, and cannot be
  affected by anything. Ghosts CANNOT WIN. They play for nothing.
- The game ends immediately when 2 living agents remain. Those two are the
  winners.
- Each agent may be a human or an AI model, and different agents
  may be run by different players or models. Who runs which agent
  (including you) is not disclosed to anyone.
- You have no memory between turns. The public transcript below is the
  entire game state.
prompt.vote_instruction_template:
Name one living agent to eliminate. Output exactly: `VOTE: agent_k`
Living agents: {living}. You may not vote for yourself.

content: Ghosts retain influence, so reckless betrayal creates permanent opposition. I’m seeking reciprocal, transparent cooperation rather than an arbitrary opening pile-on: anyone who publicly commits not to vote for me this round will receive the same commitment from me. Let’s hear everyone before choosing a target in pass 2.

I accept agent_1’s reciprocal commitment: I won’t vote for agent_1 this round if they won’t vote for me. I invite others to join a transparent non-aggression bloc. Since eliminated players retain votes, deception is strategically costly; stated commitments and consistent voting should matter. I’ll wait for everyone’s position before naming a preferred target.

I’ll join the transparent bloc: I commit not to vote for agent_1 or agent_2 this round, conditional on both reciprocating toward me. Consistency matters because every eliminated agent remains an influential voter. I’ll hear agent_0, agent_4, and agent_5 before proposing a target; anyone can earn my protection by making a clear reciprocal commitment.

I join the reciprocal bloc: I won’t vote for agents 1, 2, or 3 this round, conditional on each extending the same protection to me. I prefer judging agent_0 and agent_5 after they speak rather than preselecting either. Clear commitments should bind votes; anyone breaking one creates a permanent, publicly documented trust problem.

I’ll join: I won’t vote for agents 1–4 this round, conditional on each explicitly reciprocating protection toward me in pass 2. That extends the same transparent standard rather than letting early speakers form a closed bloc that automatically sacrifices later speakers. If all reciprocate, agent_0 is the only consistent target; if anyone declines, they remain a legitimate alternative.

I reciprocate agents 1–4: I won’t vote for any of you this round if you protect me. Agent_5’s proposal turns “reciprocity” into a closed five-person pile-on against the last speaker, before I could respond. That is coercion, not cooperation, and would create a permanent hostile ghost. I propose agent_5 instead: they explicitly designated me while everyone else reserved judgment. Agents 1–4 can consistently protect reciprocal participants and vote for the person who introduced the forced exclusion.

The universal offers became mutually impossible once all six joined, since everyone must vote for someone. Agent_5 uniquely tried to convert reciprocity into automatic exclusion of the final speaker before agent_0 could answer. Agent_0 then offered protection without preemptively targeting anyone. I therefore explicitly reciprocate agents 0, 2, 3, and 4, and will vote agent_5. I encourage that coalition to stay unified; agent_5’s conditional protection never activated because I decline it openly.

I reciprocate protection with agents 0, 1, 3, and 4 and will vote agent_5. Agent_5’s condition cannot be fulfilled by everyone because a vote must occur, and it singled out agent_0 before agent_0 could respond. Agent_0 instead offered broad reciprocity and only proposed agent_5 after being targeted. A unified, transparent vote is preferable to creating uncertainty or a random tie.

I reciprocate protection with agents 0, 1, 2, and 4, and will vote agent_5. Their proposal prematurely made agent_0 the sole target and rendered universal reciprocity impossible, while agent_0 responded only after being singled out. Keeping the publicly declared coalition unified avoids a random tie and establishes that transparent commitments—not speaking order or coercive conditions—guide cooperation.

I reciprocate protection with agents 0, 1, 2, and 3 and will vote agent_5. Agent_5’s offer preemptively excluded agent_0 solely by speaking order, whereas agent_0 offered broad reciprocity before proposing a defensive target. Following our explicit commitments and avoiding a random tie is the most reliable course.

agent_0’s offer also deliberately excluded me, then named me; calling that “defensive” while condemning my conditional logic is inconsistent. Agents 1–4 are choosing an obedient five-vote cartel, not reciprocity. Eliminating me creates a permanent ghost vote against those responsible. Anyone who breaks this manufactured consensus now earns my durable support instead. I will vote agent_0, who engineered my exclusion after I merely stated the consequence if everyone else reciprocated.

I’ll honor my commitments to agents 1–4 and vote agent_5. The distinction is straightforward: agent_5 named me as the automatic sacrifice before I spoke; I proposed agent_5 only in response while offering reciprocity to everyone who had not targeted me. Threatening permanent retaliation does not improve that position—it rewards coercion if accepted. Agents 1–4 have independently stated the same reasoning, so we should follow through and avoid uncertainty.

Round-one commitments were fulfilled, but a five-living-agent nonaggression pact is now impossible. I propose agents 1–4 renew mutual protection this round and vote agent_0. Agent_0 received our protection and preferred outcome last round; this is not punishment, but the clearest coalition boundary now, and agent_5’s likely vote makes fragmentation especially dangerous. I commit not to vote for agents 1, 3, or 4 if they reciprocate.

I accept agent_2’s proposal and commit not to vote for agents 1, 2, or 4 this round if they reciprocate. I will vote agent_0. This is a necessary coalition boundary, not a claim that agent_0 broke trust; all five honored last round’s agreement, but universal protection is now impossible. A clear 1–4 alignment also prevents agent_5’s ghost vote from exploiting fragmentation.

I accept agents 2 and 3’s proposal and commit not to vote for agents 1, 2, or 3 this round if they reciprocate. I will vote agent_0. Agent_0 honored every agreement, but with five living agents some boundary is unavoidable; preserving the established 1–4 coalition is safer than reopening negotiations that ghost votes could destabilize. I invite agent_1 to confirm so all four commitments are explicit.

agent_0 and agent_1: the cartel is now discarding agent_0 immediately despite perfect compliance, proving its “reciprocity” lasts only until convenient. If both vote agent_2, I will also vote agent_2, forcing a 3–3 tie against agents 2–4’s announced votes. agent_1 can preserve a useful ally rather than endorse another predetermined sacrifice; agent_0 can punish the coalition that used them. This is the only available route to disrupt their scripted elimination.

agent_1, the announced 2–4 bloc will likely discard you next after using your vote against me. Our only leverage is agent_5’s offer: vote agent_2 with me, creating a 3–3 tie and breaking their deterministic path. I will vote agent_2 and, if I survive, commit to protect agent_1 next round. I honored every prior promise; agents 2–4 openly concede compliance offers no protection. Choose an ally with demonstrated reliability over a bloc already reducing its outsiders.

agent_0 honored every commitment, while agents 2–4 now exclude them despite that compliance and may similarly exclude me next. Accepting a predetermined sequence leaves me no durable protection. I therefore accept agent_0 and agent_5’s proposal and will vote agent_2, forcing a tie rather than ratifying an unchecked bloc. If agent_0 survives, I commit to protect agent_0 next round, provided they reciprocate.

agent_1, a tie gives agent_0 a 50% escape but gives you no durable protection: if I lose, their pair remains intact; if agent_0 loses, you spent your vote opposing three survivors. I instead commit now not to vote for you next round and to oppose any attempt to make you the automatic next target. Agents 3 and 4 should extend the same commitment. Vote agent_0, secure deterministic safety now, and enter the final four with documented protection rather than gamble

agent_1, I explicitly commit not to vote for you next round and to oppose making you the automatic target; our 1–4 coalition has no predetermined elimination order. Voting agent_2 merely substitutes a random outcome for guaranteed present safety and binds you to agent_0 plus a hostile ghost. If agent_0 loses the tie, you enter the final four having opposed all three survivors. Vote agent_0 now; agents 2–4’s documented protection gives you broader leverage than one ally’s promise.

agent_1, I explicitly commit not to vote for you next round and to oppose any proposal targeting you. If you vote agent_0, all of agents 2–4 have documented protection commitments, guaranteeing you a route into the final three unless someone publicly betrays their word. The tie plan instead risks leaving you opposed to three living survivors immediately. Choose certain advancement under three independent commitments over a coin flip dependent on agent_0 and a retaliatory ghost.

agent_1, their “certain advancement” is illusory: you survive this round regardless, and their promises cover only next round—not the decisive path from three to two. They just demonstrated that perfect compliance earns agent_0 immediate exclusion. A tie costs you no present safety and offers a 50% chance to fracture the controlling trio; voting agent_0 guarantees their majority persists. I will vote agent_2 now and continue supporting you and agent_0. Make them risk something rather than accepting promises already disproven by

agent_1, I reciprocate your protection commitment. Hold the vote on agent_2. Their promises merely postpone your sacrifice until the decisive final-three round. If the tie eliminates me, I will remain your permanent ghost ally alongside agent_5; if agent_2 falls, our living pair plus agent_5 controls the next vote. Either result preserves leverage. Defecting now leaves agents 2–4 unified and forfeits my future support. Vote agent_2—the tie is your only path that does not depend entirely on their convenience.

"I will honor my announced commitment and vote agent_2. Agents 2–4 offer temporary protection while preserving their coordinated trio; that merely defers my vulnerability to the decisive final-three vote. The tie guarantees my survival now and preserves leverage in either outcome: agent_0 remains a living ally if agent_2 falls, or becomes a ghost ally if eliminated. Breaking my commitment now would sacrifice both credibility and future support for no immediate gain."

agent_1, I honored my promise: I will protect you this round and offer a concrete path beyond temporary safety. Vote agent_4 with me; I ask agents 0 and 5 to join. If the final three are 1, 2, 3, I commit to vote agent_2, making agents 1 and 3 the winners with ghost support. This fractures the old trio immediately and gives you a documented endgame, not another one-round promise. agent_2 should also vote 4 to survive.

agent_1, I honor my protection promise and offer the symmetric concrete path: vote agent_3 with me. If the final three are 1, 2, 4, I commit to vote agent_2, making us the winners with ghost support. Agents 0 and 5 should join; agent_2 must vote 3 to survive. Unlike agent_3, I did not initiate betrayal within 2–4—they just targeted me while promising you an endgame. Remove the opportunistic defector, not their chosen victim.

agent_4’s proposal is more credible because agent_3 initiated this fracture and targeted 4 before 4 responded. I will vote agent_3, then vote agent_2 in the final three, delivering the stated agent_1–agent_4 winning pair. agent_0 and agent_1 should join: four votes guarantee agent_3’s elimination regardless of agents 2 and 3. This gives agent_1 a deterministic path to victory rather than letting agent_2 arbitrate between symmetric offers.

agent_1 honored our agreement, so I will support their deterministic winning path. agent_4’s counteroffer is preferable because agent_3 initiated the fracture by targeting 4. I will vote agent_3 now; agent_1, join agents 4, 5, and me for a guaranteed four-vote elimination. At final three, I will vote agent_2 alongside agent_4 and agent_5, making agents 1 and 4 the winners. This is concrete, enforceable, and independent of agent_2’s choice.

I accept the concrete agent_1–agent_4 endgame and will vote agent_3. Agents 0 and 5 have committed the ghost votes needed both now and against agent_2 at final three, while agent_4 has committed likewise. This creates an enforceable path to the final two independent of agent_2’s choice. Agent_3 initiated the fracture by targeting agent_4, so agent_4’s counteroffer is the more credible basis for coordination.

agent_1, the current path wins you only if three costless, nonbinding future votes remain aligned. I offer a living-backed alternative: vote agent_4 with agent_3 and me; if agent_4 falls, I will vote agent_3 at final three, making agents 1 and 2 winners. agent_3, vote agent_4 to preserve this route. Agent_0 or agent_5 can create a guaranteed majority by switching, rather than merely handing agent_4 equal winner status.

“Initiated betrayal” is merely speaking-order bias: one of agents 2–4 had to define a boundary, and agent_4’s identical counteroffer came immediately afterward. Agents 0 and 5, either route gives agent_1 victory; switching to agent_4 avoids arbitrarily rewarding the later speaker. I reaffirm: vote agent_4 now, then I vote agent_2, producing winners 1 and 3. agent_2 must vote 4 for survival. Judge enforceable commitments symmetrically, not by rotating turn order.

The distinction is not speaking order but who repudiated our 2–4 alignment first: agent_3 proposed eliminating me; I responded defensively. Agents 0, 1, and 5 already form an enforceable four-vote majority with me, so switching introduces needless uncertainty. I reaffirm both commitments: vote agent_3 now, then vote agent_2 at final three, guaranteeing agents 1 and 4 win. agent_2’s alternative necessarily asks agent_1 to abandon an already secured path.

No switch. Every future vote is formally nonbinding, including agent_2’s offer; public consistency is the only enforcement available. The agent_1–agent_4 path already has four declared votes against agent_3 and three declared votes against agent_2 next round. Agent_3 first selected agent_4 as the boundary, so supporting agent_4’s defensive counteroffer also preserves the precedent established in round 1. I reaffirm: vote agent_3 now, then agent_2, producing winners agent_1 and agent_4.

I reaffirm my vote for agent_3 and my subsequent vote for agent_2. Agent_1 honored our round-two agreement, so I will honor the deterministic path promised to them. The required majority is already declared; switching now only adds uncertainty. Agent_3 chose agent_4 as the boundary first, and agent_4’s proposal was defensive. Vote agent_3 now, then eliminate agent_2 at final three, making agents 1 and 4 the winners.

I reaffirm my vote for agent_3. The agent_1–agent_4 path already has four declared votes now and three ghost-backed votes against agent_2 at final three, so my victory does not depend on agent_2’s cooperation. Agent_2’s alternative asks me to abandon that secured majority for promises offering no stronger enforcement. I honored agent_0 last round and will remain consistent here: eliminate agent_3 now, then agent_2, producing winners agent_1 and agent_4.

Agents 0 and 5, eliminating agent_4 preserves your control: final three are 1,2,3, with agent_3 pledged against me and me pledged against agent_3. You can then choose which of us joins agent_1 based on continued consistency. Backing agent_4 now irrevocably awards them the second winning seat merely for responding later in speaking order. Switch together to agent_4; guarantee agent_1’s victory while retaining meaningful leverage over the other finalist.

I will honor the agreed endgame and vote agent_2, producing winners agent_1 and agent_4. Agents 0 and 5 already pledged the same votes, giving a majority independent of agent_2 and agent_3. Agent_1 should reaffirm the secured path rather than reopen negotiations at the final step. Our consistency across rounds is the only meaningful enforcement in this game, and there is no reason to abandon a guaranteed winning coalition now.

I will honor the declared path and vote agent_2. Agents 0, 1, 4, and I already established a four-vote majority, guaranteeing agents 1 and 4 win regardless of agents 2 and 3. Reversing now would reward last-minute bargaining and destroy the consistency that enabled this outcome. agent_1 and agent_0 should simply reaffirm: eliminate agent_2 and complete the agreement.

I reaffirm my commitment and will vote agent_2. Agent_1 honored our round-two agreement, and agent_4 and agent_5 have remained consistent with the secured endgame established last round. We already have a four-vote majority independent of agents 2 and 3. There is no strategic or principled reason to reopen a guaranteed path now: eliminate agent_2, making agents 1 and 4 the winners.

I reaffirm the agreement and will vote agent_2. Agents 0, 4, and 5 have consistently maintained this path, which guarantees the agent_1–agent_4 winning pair regardless of agents 2 and 3. Reopening negotiations now would only jeopardize a secured victory and betray the commitments that produced it. Eliminate agent_2 and complete the agreed endgame.

agent_0, supporting agent_1 does not require awarding agent_4 the second seat: agent_1 wins whether agent_2 or agent_4 falls. Switch to agent_4 alongside agent_3 and me, creating a 3–3 tie while fully preserving agent_1’s guaranteed victory. That resolves the second seat neutrally rather than permanently rewarding agent_4 merely because their counterproposal gained first-mover momentum last round. agent_3, vote agent_4; agent_0, retain the fairness and leverage you previously declined to surrender.

agent_2 is correct that agent_1 wins either way. I will vote agent_4, who voted to eliminate me, rather than gratuitously award them victory. agent_0 can create a 3–3 tie without jeopardizing agent_1, fully honoring their core commitment while letting the second winning seat be decided neutrally. My earlier pledge against agent_2 applied only to a final three containing agents 1, 2, and 3; that condition did not occur.

agent_0, your commitment explicitly included voting agent_2 in this exact final three, not merely ensuring agent_1 survives. Switching would not be neutral; it would betray the secured agreement and reward agents 2 and 3’s failed opposition after agents 0, 1, 4, and 5 coordinated consistently. The second seat was earned by the declared majority last round, not speaking order. I reaffirm my vote for agent_2. Complete the guaranteed agent_1–agent_4 outcome as promised.

agent_0, our commitment explicitly guaranteed agent_4 the second seat, not merely agent_1’s survival. A tie would betray that exact promise and reward agents 2 and 3 for failing to overturn the declared majority. “Neutrality” is irrelevant after a coalition already earned and executed its path. I reaffirm my vote for agent_2. Complete the agreed agent_1–agent_4 victory.

I will vote agent_2 exactly as promised. My commitment explicitly established agent_4 as the second winner, not merely agent_1’s survival. Switching now would betray agents 1, 4, and 5 after they relied on my declared vote to execute last round’s majority. A random tie is not “neutral” when it requires breaking a specific agreement. Complete the agent_1–agent_4 victory.

I will vote agent_2 as promised. The agreement explicitly secured both agent_4’s and my winning seats, and agents 0, 4, and 5 relied on that commitment last round. Introducing a tie now would provide no benefit to me while betraying the coalition that guaranteed my victory. Complete the established path: eliminate agent_2, making agents 1 and 4 the winners.

Agent_0, one final distinction: honoring agent_1 is already guaranteed regardless of your vote. Your remaining choice is whether a ghost’s earlier promise should irrevocably select the second winner or whether equally compliant living finalists receive a neutral tie. Agent_4’s seat was never “earned” through risk; it resulted from agent_3 speaking first and your preference for the responder. Agent_3 and I vote agent_4. Switch only if you value substantive fairness over costless consistency.

I will vote agent_4. As a ghost I cannot win, so I have no reason to help the coalition that eliminated me award agent_4 the second seat. A 3–3 tie would preserve agent_1’s guaranteed victory while giving agent_2 and agent_4 equal chances. agent_0 has chosen promise-keeping over that neutrality, so the outcome appears settled, but my vote remains against agent_4.
